narrative:
The model predicts you have a 24% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your lack of desire to pursue higher education, your history of one past failure, and your reason for choosing this school. Wanting to continue studying after this year is the single most important factor. Every student who passed expressed a clear wish to pursue higher education; your answer of “no” pulled the prediction strongly toward failing. Your record of one previous failure was the second-biggest driver. Students who passed had zero past failures on average, so this history added a clear push toward the fail outcome. Finally, your reason for choosing the school (living nearby) worked in the opposite direction, gently pulling the prediction back toward passing, yet not enough to outweigh the other two influences.

Because the overall risk remains elevated, the school has decided you must take remedial courses. To improve your chances, think seriously about whether you truly want to continue studying beyond this year; reconnecting with that goal can be powerful. Reducing future absences, which are already much higher than the average of under four days among students who passed, and addressing any lingering gaps from your earlier failure will also help. Taking the remedial classes seriously gives you a concrete way to strengthen these areas before the final exams.
